about: One entry per rule code of Risk.RULES. The quick check reads the in-scope entries: a hypothesis, the questions that decide it, and the named mitigations a verdict must report on. Reliability wording only.

handoff-after-ack.hypothesis: Work is handed to an in-process thread after the caller gets its answer; a restart loses it and nobody retries.
handoff-after-ack.check: Does the submitted work matter to the business (not a notification or a metric)? Is the caller answered before the work is durable? Does anything re-derive the work later?

mitigations.name: future joined before response
mitigations.text: the future is joined or awaited before the response is returned

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work was persisted with a claimable state before the submit, and a sweeper or scheduler picks it up

mitigations.name: persistent job runner
mitigations.text: the executor is a persistent job runner (db-scheduler, JobRunr, Quartz with a JDBC store)

mitigations.name: partial sweeper
mitigations.text: a durable claim exists but the sweeper covers only part of the work

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the work is best effort (a comment, a name or a log that says so)

handoff-after-ack.cite: the submit line; the line that answers the caller; the line that proves or disproves the durable claim
handoff-after-ack.fix: Persist the work as a pending row in the same transaction and let a scheduled sweeper process pending rows, or do the work before answering.
handoff-after-ack.verify: Stop the JVM between the response and the task; after a restart the work must still happen.

handoff-after-consume.hypothesis: The consumer hands work to an in-process thread and returns, so the message is acknowledged before the work is done; a restart loses it and the broker never redelivers.
handoff-after-consume.check: Does the forked work matter to the business? When is the message acknowledged (auto-ack on return, manual ack)? Does anything re-derive the work later?

mitigations.name: ack after forked work
mitigations.text: the listener acknowledges manually only after the forked work completes

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work was persisted with a claimable state before the submit, and a sweeper picks it up

mitigations.name: partial sweeper
mitigations.text: a durable claim exists but the sweeper covers only part of the work

handoff-after-consume.cite: the submit line; the listener method's return or ack; the line that proves or disproves a durable claim
handoff-after-consume.fix: Do the work on the listener thread before returning, or persist it as a pending row and process it with a sweeper.
handoff-after-consume.verify: Deliver a message and stop the JVM before the forked task runs; after a restart the work must still happen.

async-in-tx.hypothesis: A task is submitted before the transaction commits; it can run before the data is visible, or after a rollback for data that never existed.
async-in-tx.check: Does the forked task read or act on what this transaction writes? Can it run before the commit or after a rollback?

mitigations.name: fork after commit
mitigations.text: the task is submitted from afterCommit, a TransactionSynchronization or an after-commit event listener

mitigations.name: task re-reads with retry
mitigations.text: the task carries only ids and re-reads the rows with a retry that waits for the commit

mitigations.name: tolerates missing row
mitigations.text: the task tolerates a missing row by retrying, but still has external effects on rollback

async-in-tx.cite: the submit line; the @Transactional or transaction start; what the task reads
async-in-tx.fix: Submit the task after the commit (TransactionSynchronization.afterCommit or @TransactionalEventListener) and pass only ids.
async-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the submit; the task must not act on the rolled-back data.

dual-write-in-tx.hypothesis: A message is sent inside the database transaction, before the commit; if the commit fails, consumers already received a message about data that does not exist.
dual-write-in-tx.check: Is the send inside the commit scope? What does a consumer do with a message whose data was rolled back? Can a retry of the caller send a second message?

mitigations.name: send after commit
mitigations.text: the send happens in afterCommit or an after-commit event listener

mitigations.name: transactional outbox
mitigations.text: the message is written to an outbox table in the same transaction and relayed later

mitigations.name: event publication registry
mitigations.text: Spring Modulith's event publication registry persists the event with the transaction

mitigations.name: consumer idempotent on business key
mitigations.text: the consumer ignores messages whose data does not exist or was already processed

dual-write-in-tx.cite: the send line; the write line; the transaction boundary
dual-write-in-tx.fix: Write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it after the commit, or send it from an after-commit hook.
dual-write-in-tx.verify: Force the commit to fail after the send; no consumer may act on the message.

dual-write.hypothesis: The database write and the message send are separate steps; a crash between them keeps one and loses the other.
dual-write.check: In which order do the write and the send happen? Who notices a lost message or a lost row? Is there a reconciliation?

mitigations.name: transactional outbox
mitigations.text: the message is written to an outbox table with the data and relayed later

mitigations.name: change data capture
mitigations.text: messages are produced from the database log, not by this code

mitigations.name: idempotent write on redelivery
mitigations.text: the send comes first and the write is idempotent when the work is redelivered

mitigations.name: reconciliation job
mitigations.text: a scheduled job compares the two sides and repairs differences

mitigations.name: consumer tolerates missing message
mitigations.text: the consumer side re-derives state, so a lost message only delays it

dual-write.cite: the write line; the send line
dual-write.fix: Use a transactional outbox, or make one side re-derivable and reconcile it on a schedule.
dual-write.verify: Stop the JVM between the write and the send; the system must converge without manual repair.

remote-in-tx.hypothesis: A remote call happens while a database transaction is open; a rollback afterwards cannot undo what the remote side did, and a slow provider holds connections.
remote-in-tx.check: Is the call a read or an operation with effects? Is the transaction really open at the call? Is the remote effect reversed when the transaction rolls back?

mitigations.name: call outside transaction
mitigations.text: the call actually runs outside the transaction (another proxy, REQUIRES_NEW ended, or no @Transactional on this path)

mitigations.name: read-only call with timeout
mitigations.text: the call only reads and has a short timeout

mitigations.name: compensation that reverses
mitigations.text: a rollback triggers a compensation that undoes the remote effect, not one that only logs

mitigations.name: persisted intent
mitigations.text: the intent is persisted before the call and a later step reconciles it

remote-in-tx.cite: the remote call; the transaction boundary; the rollback handling
remote-in-tx.fix: Move the remote call out of the transaction (before it, or after the commit with persisted intent), or add a compensation that really reverses it.
remote-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the remote call succeeds; the remote side must end up consistent.

in-memory-state.hypothesis: Business state is kept in a collection or counter of a singleton bean; it is lost on restart and differs between replicas.
in-memory-state.check: Which business fact does the collection hold? Is it also stored durably? What happens on a restart or with a second replica?

mitigations.name: durable copy
mitigations.text: the same fact is written to a durable store in the same method, or restored at startup

mitigations.name: cache with loader
mitigations.text: the collection is a cache with an expiry and a loader from a durable store

mitigations.name: restored on startup
mitigations.text: the state is rebuilt at startup, but changes since the last write are lost

mitigations.name: single replica stated
mitigations.text: the code states the application runs as one instance (recorded as an assumption)

in-memory-state.cite: the write to the collection; the durable write or its absence
in-memory-state.fix: Keep the state in the database or a shared store, and use memory only as a cache in front of it.
in-memory-state.verify: Restart the instance after a change; the state must survive.

shared-field-write.hypothesis: A request or message writes a field of a singleton bean; concurrent requests overwrite each other and the value differs between replicas.
shared-field-write.check: Is the field per-request data, or configuration set once? Can two requests interleave between the write and the read?

mitigations.name: assigned once
mitigations.text: the field is assigned once from configuration or at startup

mitigations.name: request or session scope
mitigations.text: the bean is request-, session- or prototype-scoped

mitigations.name: synchronized local use
mitigations.text: writes and reads are synchronized and the value is only used within the same call

shared-field-write.cite: the field write; the bean's scope declaration
shared-field-write.fix: Keep per-request data in local variables or method parameters, not in fields of a singleton.
shared-field-write.verify: Send two concurrent requests with different data; each must see only its own.

http-session.hypothesis: Data lives in the in-memory HTTP session; users lose it on a restart or when routed to another replica.
http-session.check: What is stored in the session? What happens when it is missing on another replica?

mitigations.name: spring session
mitigations.text: Spring Session stores the session in a shared store for this module

mitigations.name: cache of durable value
mitigations.text: the attribute only caches a value that is also stored durably

mitigations.name: missing state handled
mitigations.text: the code handles a missing attribute safely by asking the user again

http-session.cite: the session write; the read that depends on it
http-session.fix: Store the session in a shared store (Spring Session) or keep the state on the client or in the database.
http-session.verify: Restart the instance mid-flow; the user's flow must continue or restart safely.

local-file.hypothesis: A file is written to the instance's local disk and read later or by another instance; it is lost when the instance is replaced.
local-file.check: Is the file a staging buffer deleted in the same request, or is it read later or by another instance?

mitigations.name: temp file deleted
mitigations.text: the file is temporary and deleted in a finally block of the same flow

mitigations.name: uploaded in same flow
mitigations.text: the file is uploaded to shared storage within the same flow before it is needed again

mitigations.name: shared volume
mitigations.text: the path is configured as a shared, mounted volume (recorded as an assumption)

local-file.cite: the file write; the read or delete
local-file.fix: Write to shared object storage, or delete the local file before the flow ends.
local-file.verify: Replace the instance between the write and the read; the flow must still find the data.

consumer-not-idempotent.hypothesis: Brokers deliver at least once and nothing checks whether a message was already processed; a redelivery repeats the write, send or call.
consumer-not-idempotent.check: Can a message be identified (an id or business key)? Is processing keyed on it? What exactly is duplicated on redelivery?

mitigations.name: unique business key
mitigations.text: a unique constraint on a business key with conflict handling stops the duplicate

mitigations.name: processed-message table
mitigations.text: a processed-message record is checked before the work

mitigations.name: conditional update
mitigations.text: the write is a conditional update or upsert that is a no-op the second time

mitigations.name: fifo deduplication
mitigations.text: the queue deduplicates by id for a short window (SQS FIFO, 5 minutes)

consumer-not-idempotent.cite: the listener entry; the first side effect; the check or its absence
consumer-not-idempotent.fix: Record the message id (or business key) with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and skip duplicates.
consumer-not-idempotent.verify: Deliver the same message twice; the side effects must happen once.

webhook-not-idempotent.hypothesis: Providers retry webhooks, and nothing checks the provider's event id; a retry repeats the side effects.
webhook-not-idempotent.check: Which provider id identifies the delivery? Is it checked before the work, or protected by a unique constraint? What is duplicated?

mitigations.name: unique event id
mitigations.text: a unique constraint on the provider event id with conflict handling stops the duplicate

mitigations.name: lookup before write
mitigations.text: the code looks up the event id before doing the work and skips known ones

mitigations.name: harmless duplicates
mitigations.text: duplicates only cost storage, and everything downstream is idempotent

webhook-not-idempotent.cite: the handler entry; the first side effect; the id check or its absence
webhook-not-idempotent.fix: Store the provider event id with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and return success for duplicates.
webhook-not-idempotent.verify: Send the same event twice; the side effects must happen once.

webhook-sync-remote.hypothesis: The webhook calls another service before answering; a slow dependency makes the provider time out and retry while the first attempt still runs.
webhook-sync-remote.check: How long can the remote call take? Does the provider retry while the first attempt runs, and is the handler idempotent?

mitigations.name: short timeout and idempotent handler
mitigations.text: the remote call has a short timeout and the handler is idempotent on the event id

webhook-sync-remote.cite: the remote call; its timeout configuration or absence
webhook-sync-remote.fix: Acknowledge after persisting the event, and make the remote call from a durable, retried step.
webhook-sync-remote.verify: Delay the remote side beyond the provider's timeout; the work must happen once.

job-without-lock.hypothesis: A scheduled job runs on every instance; with more than one replica it repeats its writes and sends.
job-without-lock.check: With two replicas, what is duplicated? Are the steps row-locked or idempotent?

mitigations.name: distributed lock
mitigations.text: ShedLock, a Quartz JDBC store or leader election guards the job, through code the scanner missed

mitigations.name: row claim or upsert
mitigations.text: every write claims rows (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) or is an upsert

mitigations.name: idempotent by comment
mitigations.text: comments state the steps are idempotent, without code that enforces it

job-without-lock.cite: the @Scheduled method; the first write or send; the lock or its absence
job-without-lock.fix: Guard the job with ShedLock or a database lock, or make each step claim its rows.
job-without-lock.verify: Run two instances at the scheduled time; the work must happen once.

proxy-bypassed.hypothesis: A method calls its own @Async or @Transactional method through this; the proxy never sees the call, so it runs synchronously or without the transaction.
proxy-bypassed.check: Which annotation is bypassed? Does it matter here (@Async always; @Transactional only when the target writes or sends)?

mitigations.name: self-injected proxy
mitigations.text: the call goes through a self-injected proxy or AopContext.currentProxy()

mitigations.name: caller transactional
mitigations.text: the caller is itself transactional, so the work still runs in a transaction

proxy-bypassed.cite: the self-call; the annotation on the target
proxy-bypassed.fix: Move the annotated method to another bean, or call it through the proxy.
proxy-bypassed.verify: Assert in a test that the target runs on another thread or in a transaction.

async-listener.hypothesis: An event listener runs asynchronously; the event exists only in memory until it runs, so a restart drops it.
async-listener.check: Is the listener's work required? Is the event persisted anywhere?

mitigations.name: event publication registry
mitigations.text: Spring Modulith's event publication registry persists the event

mitigations.name: re-derivable by sweeper
mitigations.text: a sweeper re-derives the listener's work from durable state

mitigations.name: best-effort listener
mitigations.text: the listener's work is best effort by the code's own statement

async-listener.fix: Persist the event (outbox or Modulith registry) or make the work re-derivable.
async-listener.verify: Stop the JVM after publishing; the listener's work must still happen.

handoff-in-listener.hypothesis: A listener hands work to an in-process thread and returns; if the instance stops before the work runs, it is lost.
handoff-in-listener.check: Is the forked work required? Does anything re-derive it?

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work is persisted with a claimable state and a sweeper picks it up

handoff-in-listener.cite: the submit line; the listener method
handoff-in-listener.fix: Do the work in the listener, or persist it and process it with a sweeper.
handoff-in-listener.verify: Stop the JVM before the forked task runs; the work must still happen.

handoff-in-job.hypothesis: A scheduled job forks work onto other threads; a shutdown drops what is still queued, and the next run may not pick it up.
handoff-in-job.check: What is queued when a shutdown hits? Does the next run pick it up?

mitigations.name: re-derived every run
mitigations.text: the job re-derives its work from durable state on every run

mitigations.name: drains on shutdown
mitigations.text: the executor waits for queued tasks on shutdown

handoff-in-job.cite: the submit line; how the job selects its work
handoff-in-job.fix: Select work from durable state on every run and mark it done only after it completes.
handoff-in-job.verify: Stop the JVM mid-run; the next run must finish the work.

notification-in-tx.hypothesis: A notification goes out from another thread while the transaction is still open; users can be told about a change that rolls back.
notification-in-tx.check: Can the user be told about a change that later rolls back? Is that acceptable for this notification?

mitigations.name: sent after commit
mitigations.text: the notification is sent after the commit

mitigations.name: best-effort notification
mitigations.text: the notification is informational and a wrong one is harmless

notification-in-tx.cite: the notification submit; the transaction boundary
notification-in-tx.fix: Send the notification after the commit.
notification-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the notification is queued; no user may be notified.

notification-handoff.hypothesis: A message to users (e-mail, SMS, chat) is sent on another thread after the work returns; a restart loses the ones still queued.
notification-handoff.check: Must the user get this notification, or is it best effort? Is it recorded durably before the hand-off? Does anything resend a lost one?

mitigations.name: persisted notification
mitigations.text: the notification is stored (an outbox row or a queue message) before the hand-off, and a job or consumer sends it

mitigations.name: send awaited
mitigations.text: the future of the send is joined or awaited before the work returns

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the notification is best effort (a comment, a name or a log that says so)

notification-handoff.cite: the hand-off line; the send; the durable record or its absence
notification-handoff.fix: Store the notification in the same transaction as the change and send it from a job or a broker consumer, or state that losing it is acceptable.
notification-handoff.verify: Stop the instance right after the operation returns; the notification must still go out, or its loss must be accepted.

timer-handoff.hypothesis: Work is scheduled to run later on an in-process timer; if the instance restarts before it fires, the work never happens.
timer-handoff.check: Does the delayed work matter to the business? Is the due work stored anywhere durable? Does a startup hook or a scheduled job pick up what was missed?

mitigations.name: persisted schedule
mitigations.text: the due work is stored with its time, and a scheduled job or a startup hook runs what is due

mitigations.name: re-derived on startup
mitigations.text: a startup hook or a scheduled job re-derives the pending work from durable state

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the delayed work is best effort, such as a cache refresh or a reminder that may be skipped

timer-handoff.cite: the schedule call; where the due work is stored, or its absence
timer-handoff.fix: Store the due work with its time and run it from a scheduled job or a persistent scheduler (Quartz with a JDBC store, db-scheduler, JobRunr).
timer-handoff.verify: Schedule the work, restart the instance before it fires; it must still run.

async-response.hypothesis: The handler returns a Mono, future or emitter and the client waits; a restart fails the request, and a client that retries may repeat work the first attempt already did.
async-response.check: Does the asynchronous work write, send or call out? Can a retried request repeat that? Is the work durable before the response completes?

mitigations.name: reads only
mitigations.text: the asynchronous work only reads; a retry repeats nothing

mitigations.name: idempotent by key
mitigations.text: writes and sends are keyed by a request or business id, so a retried request does not repeat them

mitigations.name: durable before response
mitigations.text: the work is committed before the response completes, so a failed response leaves a consistent state

async-response.cite: the returned future or publisher; the writes and sends it performs; the key or check that makes a retry safe, or its absence
async-response.fix: Make the asynchronous writes idempotent by a request id, or commit the work before completing the response.
async-response.verify: Kill the instance while the request is in flight, retry it; the end state must match one successful request.

background-thread.hypothesis: A thread or recurring task started at startup or shutdown does work that a restart interrupts; work in flight is lost or repeated.
background-thread.check: What does the thread do: housekeeping or business work? Is it stopped cleanly on shutdown? Is its work reconstructed from durable state after a restart?

mitigations.name: housekeeping only
mitigations.text: the work is per-instance housekeeping (metrics, cache refresh, connection keep-alive) whose loss changes no business state

mitigations.name: work is durable
mitigations.text: the work it processes is read from durable state and marked done there, so a restart resumes it

mitigations.name: stopped on shutdown
mitigations.text: the thread or executor is shut down and drained in @PreDestroy, SmartLifecycle.stop or a shutdown hook

background-thread.cite: where the thread starts; what it does; how it stops
background-thread.fix: Drive the work from durable state (claimed rows, a queue) and stop the thread cleanly on shutdown.
background-thread.verify: Stop the instance while the thread is working; after restart nothing may be lost or done twice.

in-memory-cache.hypothesis: A cache, counter or lock map lives in instance memory; that is wrong when it is the only copy of a fact, or when replicas must agree on it.
in-memory-cache.check: Is the value derived from a durable source, or is memory its only copy? Do replicas need the same value (rate limits, locks, sequence numbers)?

mitigations.name: derived data
mitigations.text: every value can be recomputed from a durable source, such as a cache with a loader

mitigations.name: shared store
mitigations.text: the structure is backed by a shared store (Redis, Hazelcast, the database)

mitigations.name: single replica stated
mitigations.text: the code states the application runs as one instance (recorded as an assumption)

in-memory-cache.cite: the write to the in-memory structure; its durable source, or its absence
in-memory-cache.fix: Keep facts that matter in a shared store, and use memory only as a cache that can be rebuilt.
in-memory-cache.verify: Run two replicas or restart one; the value must agree or be rebuilt correctly.

event-in-tx.hypothesis: An in-process event is published inside a transaction; plain @EventListener methods run before the commit and may act on data that then rolls back.
event-in-tx.check: Which listeners handle the event? Do they act outside the transaction (send, call, notify, another data source)? Do they run before the commit?

mitigations.name: after-commit listeners
mitigations.text: every listener of the event is a @TransactionalEventListener after commit, or registers its work after the commit

mitigations.name: same transaction only
mitigations.text: the listeners only change data inside the same transaction, which rolls back with it

mitigations.name: idempotent reaction
mitigations.text: the listener's outside effect is checked or keyed, so acting on a rolled-back change is harmless

event-in-tx.cite: the publish; the transaction boundary; each listener's outside effect
event-in-tx.fix: Handle the event with @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT), or publish it through an outbox.
event-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the publish; no listener may have acted outside the transaction.

read-verb-writes.hypothesis: A GET or HEAD request writes or sends; clients, proxies and crawlers retry and prefetch these freely, so the write repeats.
read-verb-writes.check: What does the write change? Is it the same on every call? Could a crawler or a prefetch trigger it?

mitigations.name: same result on repeat
mitigations.text: the write sets the same value on every call (an upsert of the same row), so a repeat changes nothing

mitigations.name: access record only
mitigations.text: the write only records the access (audit log, last-seen time), where repeats are harmless

read-verb-writes.cite: the HTTP verb; the write or send
read-verb-writes.fix: Move the change to a POST, PUT or PATCH, or make it idempotent.
read-verb-writes.verify: Call the GET twice; the state must not change the second time.

no-hint.hypothesis: The scan matched no failure pattern on this operation, although it writes, sends or calls out. A rule may have missed one.
no-hint.check: Read the entry method and the listed effects. Is the caller answered before the work is durable? Can a retry or redelivery repeat a write, send or call? Is a remote call or send inside a transaction? Can a crash split a write from a send? Is a fact kept only in memory?
no-hint.cite: the lines that show the failure, or the lines that make the path safe
no-hint.fix: Fix it as the named rule's task says.
no-hint.verify: Verify it as the named rule's task says.
